bibliographic.title: Learning to Rate Player Positioning in Soccer

scope.rationale: Paper learns a value function over multiplayer positionings (game states) from tracking data using deep reinforcement learning; this is an off-ball/state-valuation method directly relevant to the action/state valuation literature.

model.name: Deep RL player positioning value function (Dick & Brefeld)
inputs: x/y positions of all 22 players at 25 fps
partial speeds (sx, sy) movement vectors of all players
ball possession indicator (+1/-1) for which team has the ball
image-like 9-channel tensor representation (positions of left-to-right team, right-to-left team, ball; x,y speeds for each team; ball x,y speeds)
model.target: Value function V(s) = expected discounted return G(s_t) over an episode, where reward is 1 if the ball possession episode ends in a 'success action' (team carries ball into final 25 m of opponent half, or into 18 m area around opponent goal in alternative scenario) and 0 otherwise
model.architecture: Deep convolutional neural network: three convolutional layers with 32 kernels of size 6x6 and ReLU activations, followed by a fully connected layer of 256 nodes with ReLU, and a single output node V; trained with TD(lambda) (lambda-return) batch reinforcement learning
model.spatial_resolution: continuous (x,y) rasterised into a 9-channel image-like tensor of width x height pixels
model.temporal_horizon: until end of ball-possession episode (episode terminates when team loses ball, play stops, or a 'success action' is performed)

baselines: trivial baseline using ball's distance from the goal as a measure of dangerousness (AUC = 0.5 diagonal line)
evaluation.splits: Leave-one-game-out (LOGO) cross-validation: train on four games, test on the remaining game; episodes are flipped in x and/or y during training for data augmentation

claims.statement: Even 13 seconds before the end of a possession phase, the AUC is still strictly above 0.5, indicating the learned value function captures positioning information well beyond uninformed guessing.

The first success scenario (final 25 m) yields 380 successful episodes and 715 unsuccessful episodes with an overall of 11,045 states; the second scenario (18 m around opponent goal) yields 224 successful episodes and 866 unsuccessful episodes with 11,340 states.
Using only positional information performs worse than using all available information (positions + movement vectors), though the differences are not significant in Figure 3.
Discount factor gamma = 0.95 and lambda = 0.7 (chosen via grid-search) were used; batch size of 30 episodes and the Adam optimizer; early stopping via LOGO cross-validation on the training set.
Average AUC ranges from approximately 0.85 (3 seconds before end of episode) down to approximately 0.65 (15 seconds before end) for the Movements + 25 m success scenario.
The approach easily beats a trivial baseline using ball's distance from the goal as a measure of dangerousness, which would yield AUC = 0.5.
Authors claim this work constitutes the first purely data-driven approach to machines that read and understand games and thus bridges the gap toward computational tactics.

limitations: Experiments are based on only five games of topflight European soccer.
The second success measure (18 m around the goal) has a reduced number of positive training episodes and increased influence of chance on the outcomes, leading to comparable but noisier AUC results.
Authors are not focusing on learning optimal controllers (i.e., not modelling how players should behave optimally) but only how good real players' behaviour is.
open_questions: Correlations between the dangerousness metric and traditional performance indicators like playing speed, passing, or expansion of teams could be used to group historic episodes against an opponent.

Such groups could be used to automatically devise strategic insights for an opponent (e.g., indicating that counterattacks were more promising than slow play-making or that cross passes led to more dangerous situations) and implemented in the respective game plan.
